Results show that decomposition does not universally improve patch quality; its main benefit is controlling when patch generation is attempted. It helps models prone to missing smells and can reduce overhead by gating patches. Once a smell is correctly detected, clean refactoring is generally effective, making detection the main end-to-end bottleneck. However, false positives can trigger unnecessary edits to execution-relevant constructs. Practical CI/CD agents thus need reliable abstention and construct-aware validation alongside patch generation.

fresh.title: FIRE: Failure Isolation and Reliability for Production-Connected Experiments at Scale
fresh.summary: Pre-production changes are usually tested in isolated environments to prevent their side effects from reaching production. Some record-and-replay platforms allow a production-connected mode: candidate changes receive recorded production requests while selected downstream calls reach production dependencies. This improves fidelity before deployment, but it also introduces reliability risks. At hyperscale, experimental traffic can fan out across shared services, trigger latent defects, or send malformed input to systems serving user requests. In this paper, we show how production-connected experimentation can operate reliably in a large-scale recommendation serving system. To contain downstream effects without sacrificing realistic dependency behavior, the platform uses three complementary guardrails. Isolated tiers redirect replay traffic away from shared dependencies where replication is practical. Dependency monitors observe downstream health and experiment-attributed errors and terminate experiments after sustained violations. Traffic pinning limits experimental calls to a designated subset of downstream workers when full replication would require scarce capacity. Isolated ranking tiers process billions of replayed requests per day using under 1% of the corresponding serving capacity. Over 90 days, these tiers experienced more than 200,000 abnormal worker exits without directly affecting production-serving workers. During a separate three-month window, dependency monitors cancelled approximately 5% of experiments for the measured ranking service and accounted for 87% of its cancellations. Dependency-aware triggering also reduced code-review experiment executions by 25%. These results show that high-fidelity, production-connected experimentation can operate at scale when downstream effects are isolated where possible, bounded where necessary, and continuously monitored and attributed.

fresh.title: JoyFrontBench: Evaluating Front-End Coding Agents through Goal-Oriented Acceptance Contracts
fresh.summary: Front-end coding agents are expected to produce applications that fulfill user goals, yet high task scores can coexist with failures in essential workflows. Evaluating these agents therefore requires an explicit distinction between partial implementation and application success. We introduce JoyFrontBench, a benchmark that makes this distinction through goal-oriented acceptance contracts. Each contract identifies core tasks and mandatory criteria before generation: a core task passes only when all mandatory criteria are satisfied and a shared completion threshold is met, while application success requires every core task to pass on the same operational artifact within a single run. Derived from practitioner requirements, JoyFrontBench comprises 100 front-end development problems, 764 tasks, and 2,596 atomic criteria, with reviewed annotations linking user goals to core tasks and evidence requirements. The evaluation framework combines evidence-grounded judgments with deterministic record auditing and fixed scoring rules, preserving graded task assessment alongside explicit core-task and application-level acceptance. We evaluate five coding models under two agent harnesses, OpenHands and OpenCode, on the 70-problem test set; the remaining 30 problems form a public set for validation and diagnostic analyses. Under OpenHands, the mean Average Task Score (ATS) across models is 87.69%, while the mean Application Success Rate (ASR) is 51.52%. Further analyses reveal changes in model rankings across harnesses and variation in application success across repeated runs. These findings highlight the limitations of aggregate task scores in characterizing application success and motivate explicit assessment of core-goal fulfillment alongside graded task performance.

fresh.title: LOHRE: Execution-Grounded Type Recovery via LLM-Orchestrated Hybrid Analysis
fresh.summary: Documenting stripped binary functions for security analysis requires recovering function interfaces and user-defined type (UDT) layouts from machine code. Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods face two limitations: they lack execution-based validation to detect inferred UDTs inconsistent with actual memory layouts, and may overlook evidence about shared UDTs across functions without direct call relationships. We present LLM-Orchestrated Hybrid Reverse Engineering (LOHRE), a framework that treats inferred UDTs as falsifiable hypotheses and tests them against program execution. LOHRE uses a hypothesize-validate-refine loop to test candidate layouts through paired dynamic slice emulation of baseline and mutated inputs. To reduce the cost of processing lengthy execution histories, the Execution-Depth Heuristic (EDH) compresses paired traces into an execution-depth difference and a summary of the tested field's observed uses. A cross-function knowledge base aggregates compatible UDT hypotheses and field-level confidence scores to guide testing and hypothesis refinement. We evaluate LOHRE on RealType at four optimization levels and a Windows remote procedure call (RPC) dataset. LOHRE achieves an average UDT Structural accuracy of 57.85% across RealType's four optimization levels and 35.6% on Windows RPC, outperforming the evaluated static baselines. Disabling dynamic validation reduces accuracy to 19.28% on RealType and 9.2% on Windows RPC. Removing the cross-function knowledge base reduces accuracy to 41.03% on RealType and 10.0% on Windows RPC. Replacing EDH's compressed feedback with full execution traces reduces recovery accuracy while increasing token use by 3.7 times and runtime by 3.0 times. These results indicate that execution-based validation, compact feedback, and cross-function evidence contribute to accurate and efficient UDT recovery.

fresh.title: TSBugs Explorer: Exploring and Benchmarking TypeScript Bugs
fresh.summary: Curated datasets of real-world software bugs support empirical research in software testing, debugging, and automated program repair. However, exploring heterogeneous bug collections, comparing fault characteristics across projects, and constructing research-specific subsets often require manual inspection and custom scripts. We present TSBugs Explorer, an interactive visual analytics platform built upon our previously-published dataset of 633 bugs from 16 open-source TypeScript repositories, classified into 11 fault categories. The platform integrates bug records, repository characteristics, dependency information, and taxonomy guidance through coordinated visualizations, interactive filtering, and detailed bug inspection. It supports alternative aggregation and normalization of fault distributions, pairwise repository comparisons, and analysis of differences in observed fault profiles. An integrated benchmark builder allows researchers to select bug subsets using multiple criteria, inspect their composition, and export records in CSV or JSON format. We demonstrate the platform through three research workflows: fault characterization, cross-repository comparison, and task-specific benchmark construction. Functional validation by two authors confirmed selection correctness, visualization consistency, export integrity, and reproducibility across the tested workflows. By making the existing corpus easier to explore, compare, and reuse, TSBugs Explorer facilitates systematic, research-specific selection and export of TypeScript bug records.

fresh.title: Caprese: Change Impact Recommendation Using History and Runtime Analysis
fresh.summary: Change impact recommendation identifies program entities potentially affected by source code changes. Historical co-changes and runtime dependencies provide complementary evidence, particularly in JavaScript, where dynamic and asynchronous behaviour complicates dependency analysis. We present Caprese, an open-source framework for function-level change impact recommendation in Node.js. Given a change set, it produces a ranked impact set of potentially affected functions. It supports repository-based recommendation through confidence-guided mining of recurring, change-set-relevant co-change patterns of varying lengths; dynamic recommendation through execution-derived dependencies involving calls, callbacks, events, timers, and shared state; and hybrid recommendation integrating both analyses. Its modular implementation supports reusable analyses. Evaluation on ten open-source applications and 100 selected change sets shows that, on average across projects, 77.4% of the relevant functions among the top 60 hybrid recommendations are identified exclusively by one analysis, demonstrating substantial complementarity. Dynamic recommendation achieves the highest mean precision among the top five recommendations (0.65), while repository-based recommendation performs best when the ranking is extended to 60 recommendations (0.42). Hybrid recommendation outperforms TARMAQ on average but does not consistently outperform the individual modes. Caprese is publicly available with source code, documentation, and evaluation artifacts.

fresh.title: Typify: A Tool for Usage-driven Type Inference in Python
fresh.summary: Python's dynamic type system, while expressive and flexible, creates significant challenges for static analysis tools in unannotated or partially annotated codebases. Existing approaches either require pre-existing type annotations, or depend on deep learning models that demand large training corpora and significant computational resources. We present Typify, a lightweight, usage-driven static type inference engine that infers precise type information across entire Python projects without annotations or training data. Typify integrates symbolic execution, fixpoint analysis, and context-matching retrieval to propagate types across modules, functions, and recursive call structures. The tool is available as both a command-line interface (CLI) for batch inference, evaluation and downstream integration with other tools, and a Visual Studio Code (VS Code) extension for interactive type assistance. Evaluation on the ManyTypes4Py and Typilus datasets shows that Typify outperforms all static baselines and closely matches state-of-the-art hybrid deep learning approaches, while running approximately 10x faster.

fresh.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
fresh.summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

fresh.title: Mach2: Scientific Discovery Platform with Deterministic Execution Constraints
fresh.summary: Language-model agents can formulate workflows and invoke specialized tools, yet compliance with natural-language operating rules is not guaranteed by prompting alone. Mach2 addresses this limitation by coupling Eigen orchestration to deterministic, lint-like checks of tool requests, source changes, acceptance tests, and artifact contracts. Domain requirements are represented as executable predicates: mandatory failures prevent advancement of the checked operation, while diagnostic findings are retained for correction or review. User-specified test-driven development (TDD), CodeGrapher's abstract-syntax-tree analysis, and history-guided evolutionary search provide complementary verification and optimization mechanisms. Mach2 also generates task-specific agent packages for execution through independently selected endpoints. The originating harness validates returned artifacts against declared interfaces and evidence requirements without assuming continuous supervision of the remote run. Model-internal-knowledge (MIK) dependencies are recorded separately from source-grounded and test-supported findings. This paper formalizes the rule-gated execution model and the agent-package lifecycle, and proposes measurable criteria for evaluating rule compliance, engineering validity, and cross-endpoint task continuity.

fresh.title: Where Should the Code Go? Locating Foundation-Model Errors in Bitemporal Inventory Simulation
fresh.summary: Operational reports carry two clocks: when an event happened and when its report arrived; later reports can revise earlier ones. A foundation-model component that maintains the state supported by the reports visible at a cutoff, then rolls a supplied scenario forward, can be helped by exact code before it, after it or inside the call, or asked to reason harder. We ask which remedy removes which error, for which models, on an exactly solvable lost-sales inventory environment: 36,672 independently rescored requests over twelve configurations of closed and open-weight models, with a forced-answer-call interface as a control and protocols frozen before the calls. Weak models fail in separable ways. Canonical input removes report-selection error, exact continuation removes rollout error, neither repairs the other, and which error dominates differs by model; strong models are at ceiling on raw reports. Asking for more reasoning is no substitute and can depend on the interface: under a forced answer call high effort collapses GPT-5.4 mini and DeepSeek V4 Pro, which gain or hold under automatic choice; on its provider the forced call disables reasoning for DeepSeek V4 Flash; and at high effort gpt-oss exhausts its output budget. The contribution is a controlled component diagnostic, released with every request, and evidence that for some model and provider pairs the tool-calling interface confounds reasoning evaluation.

fresh.title: Outcome Over Learning? Evidence from Student Use of AI Code Assistants for Unit Test Writing
fresh.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) code assistants are rapidly being adopted in programming education, yet little is known about how students naturally use these tools when given unrestricted access. In a user study investigating AI-assisted unit test writing, we observed that a majority of students adopted a one-shot interaction strategy, asking the AI to generate a complete unit test directly from the initial requirements. While this approach is capable of efficiently producing a solution, it shifts students' focus from learning how to write effective unit tests to simply completing the task. Moreover, because students rarely engaged in critically evaluating, refining, or iterating on AI-generated output, they may be missing opportunities to develop the critical thinking skills that are essential for effective and responsible use of AI. In an effort to shift student focus from outcome to learning we also discuss how training, accountability and improved learning task design can better support a more learning-centric responsible use of AI.

fresh.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
fresh.summary: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.

fresh.title: Discovering the Relation Between Architectural Models and Reference Architectures
fresh.summary: Assessing whether concrete software architectures are consistent with their reference architecture (RA) is essential to ensure that architectural decisions scale coherently across projects, preserving the quality attributes the RA was designed to guarantee. In the absence of dedicated techniques, mapping the components of an architectural model onto a predefined RA can be addressed only with general-purpose model-comparison algorithms. Our experiments show that these algorithms are inaccurate when applied to RAs. To address this gap, we propose Reference Architecture Mapping Discovery (RAMD), an LLM-based workflow that combines model analysis with structured prompting, and refines results through an iterative RA compliance-checking mechanism. We evaluate RAMD on 64 open-source architectural models spanning three RAs from the IoT, self-driving, and smart parking domains. With domain knowledge and GPT-4o, RAMD reaches 85.8% mapping accuracy and outperforms the strongest baseline by 44.6 percentage points, while ensuring structural consistency with the RA.

fresh.title: Operational limits of reference renewal for retained quantum-service results
fresh.summary: We implement reference renewal to reconsider retained physical quantum-service results under a prespecified protocol. Twelve transitions retained six results each; ten completed renewal, eight met the prespecified endpoint, and five succeeded using retained results alone. The exact one-sided p=0.0546875 does not establish the recovery hypothesis. Incomplete references, binding failures and sequential waits expose operational limits. Offline reconstruction recovers decisions from preserved counts. Retrospective binding-plus-oracle checking accepts all 60 usable-transition results without renewal. With the exact oracle also supplying calibration scores, the study does not demonstrate incremental numerical-correctness utility of renewal.

fresh.title: Reliable and explainable analysis of AVS/RS by Statistical Model Checking and Process Mining
fresh.summary: Automated Vehicle Storage and Retrieval Systems (AVS/RS) are increasingly adopted to boost warehouse throughput while containing operational costs. We present a tool-supported analysis workflow that combines discrete-event simulation, Statistical Model Checking (SMC), and Process Mining (PM) techniques to quantify and explain AVS/RS performance. SMC, implemented through the MultiVeStA tool, delivers statistically reliable estimates of key indicators, such as cycle times and inventory consolidation, across alternative stocking and picking policies with user-specified confidence levels. MultiVeStA orchestrates multiple independent simulations in a black-box manner, enabling automated verification. PM ingests the resulting event logs to uncover the behavioural patterns and bottlenecks that drive those indicators, closing the interpretability gap typical of simulation studies. We instantiate the framework on a new open-source AVS/RS simulator configured according to recent industrial guidelines and evaluate multiple control strategies and different scenarios. Results show that the coordinated use of SMC and PM supports both predictive what-if analyses and post-hoc diagnostics. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of a combined SMC-PM workflow to AVS/RS operations, complemented by a reusable open-source simulation and analysis toolchain.

fresh.title: How Well Do SAST Tools Work Across Languages? An Empirical Study Using OCPP Implementations
fresh.summary: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption accelerates globally, securing electric vehicle charging station (EVCS) software becomes increasingly critical. The Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP), widely adopted for EVCS management, places significant responsibility on developers to securely implement specifications that are subject to multiple interpretations. The variety of OCPP implementations across different programming languages provides a unique opportunity to evaluate security tooling in a real-world, multi-language context where implementation variability may introduce vulnerabilities. This study provides the first empirical evaluation of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tool performance across multiple programming languages using OCPP implementations as a real-world test corpus. We applied both comprehensive multi-language tools (SonarQube and Semgrep) and language-specific analyzers to twelve OCPP 1.6 implementations--each written in a distinct programming language--to examine how detection patterns vary across language ecosystems. Total issues ranged from just two in Rust to 1,689 in Java. Mature programming languages like Java yielded substantially more findings than newer languages like Rust, likely because established languages have more developed SAST tool ecosystems rather than inherently worse code quality. These results suggest that developers should consider available SAST tooling when selecting implementation languages for security critical systems.

fresh.title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
fresh.summary: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. Across 12 tasks spanning three mobile LLMs and four engine--backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, EngineAgent achieves 75% end-to-end success with either of two underlying LLMs, versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline. Success requires compilation, on-device execution, and output-logit agreement with reference implementations. EngineAgent also reduces average per-task time and model-API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.

fresh.title: An Empirical Study on CVE-based Vulnerabilities Propagation from one System to another System (IntraProject vs InterProject)
fresh.summary: Vulnerabilities in applications, including browsers, media players, online services and document readers, etc. are often exploited and cause a serious damage. The vulnerabilities could exist in your system maybe because of some coding errors, design oversights, outdated software, AI generated codes or maybe transferred from another system during development (e.g., code clones). The propagation of software vulnerabilities is a critical concern in cybersecurity. This study examines the root cause problem of vulnerabilities propagation with experiments. We analyzed the propagation of CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) based vulnerabilities within and between different software projects (IntraProject vs. InterProject). We performed several experiments on CVE based vulnerability dataset (retrieved from NVD source) by using our vulnerability detection tool (SQVDT). In the results, we discovered similar patterns of vulnerable code in several very famous recently used software, including latest version of Linux, Android operating systems, and in thousands of open source projects available on GitHub. We found several very high severity level (CVSS) vulnerabilities that propagated from one system to another system, just because of copy/paste (reuse) the code. Furthermore, we performed an empirical evaluation and verification of these vulnerable patterns that propagated to other systems by also considering the frequency of their propagation. Finlay, we recommended the impact of these vulnerabilities propagation on the interconnected systems.

fresh.title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification
fresh.summary: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. However, these approaches typically constrain the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop, in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. We introduce ProofCoder, an agentic proof-synthesis system for Rocq that approaches theorem proving from a coding-agent perspective. Rather than generating tactics within a fixed loop, ProofCoder reasons continuously throughout proof search and uses proof-assistant feedback to decide when to gather additional information, inspect proof states, revise previously generated proof fragments, or backtrack to an earlier point in the proof. This allows it to iteratively construct, repair, and refine proofs, at either tactic-level or whole-proof granularity. We evaluate ProofCoder on 280 challenging verification tasks from the AutoRocq Benchmark. On the best-performing configurations, ProofCoder increases proof success from 47% to 60% over the state-of-theart AutoRocq system, corresponding to a 27.7% relative improvement at approximately half the cost. Our ablations identify continuous reasoning as a key design choice: without it, the agent solves fewer lemmas at substantially higher cost, backtracks four to six times more often, and more frequently discards its own revisions. Whole-proof and tactic-level generation achieve similar success rates but follow distinct search and repair strategies. These results suggest that effective automated software verification requires more than improved tactic selection: continuous reasoning and feedback-guided proof revision are critical ingredients for robust proof synthesis.

fresh.title: DEIA: Evidence-Grounded Crash Repair with Change-Aware Test Design for HarmonyOS ArkTS
fresh.summary: Mobile crash repair requires more than identifying a source edit. Developers must establish how the edit relates to the reported failure and whether the modified application can be built, launched, and exercised without disrupting valid behavior. In HarmonyOS applications, this assessment also depends on platform-specific packaging and runtime execution. To address this need, we present DEIA, an evidence-grounded workflow for HarmonyOS crash repair. DEIA constructs a bounded source-evidence package, uses a large language model to propose content-anchored edits, and relies on a deterministic writer to materialize and check the patch. It derives fail-to-pass (F2P) obligations from the reported fault and pass-to-pass (P2P) obligations from the potential impact of the patch. A stage-level ledger links the patch, test obligations, runtime observations, and candidate-generation cost. We evaluate DEIA on 30 repair tasks from 24 HarmonyOS applications and compare it with an OpenHands-based workflow on 29 matched tasks. DEIA's first-added-line location exactly matches the curated reference in 25/29 tasks (86.2%), compared with 19/29 (65.5%) for OpenHands, a difference of 20.7 percentage points. DEIA also uses 81.5% fewer tokens, makes 60.8% fewer model calls, and takes 34.9% less candidate-generation time on average. Only two of the 58 behavior-specific P2P obligations were executed, both for one repair pattern; comprehensive behavior preservation therefore remains unestablished.

fresh.title: Software Refactoring Research with Large Language Models: A Systematic Literature Review
fresh.summary: Background: Code refactoring is the improvement of code internally without changing the external functionalities of the program. Due to its exhaustive nature, developers often avoid manually refactoring code. Researchers have since looked into utilizing LLMs to automate the task of refactoring. Aim and Method: Despite the promising results, there is a lack of clear un- derstanding of LLMs' effectiveness in automated refactoring. Result: From our literature review we found that: (i) there are various tools that different studies use to enhance and study LLM-driving refactoring, with tools that were used to detect code smells, generate code bases, and compare refactoring outcomes. (ii) Various datasets were collected from multiple open- source projects in multiple programming languages for analysis. These platforms included GitHub, Apache, and F-Droid, with the most popular language collec- ted and analyzed being Java. (iii) One-Shot, Few-Shot, Context-Specific, and Chain-of-Thought prompting methods have been shown to be the most effective depending on the language used. In some instances, being capable of reducing code smell by up to 89%. (iv) The definition of "accuracy" varies significantly across the literature surveyed, as this depends on the context of the study, thus calling for a need to have a standardized measurement for Accuracy. (v) The most often mentioned code smells were Large Class and Long Method, with a lot of studies also not specifying, while the most often applied refactoring type is Extract Method, showing promising results in using LLM to perform this refactoring type. (vi) When working with LLMs, they often generate erroneous code, struggle with more complex refactoring, and often misunderstand the developers' requests and miss refactoring requests.

fresh.title: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence
fresh.summary: Optimized floating-point inference is not reproducible across environments: the same model on different hardware, compilers or thread counts can produce different bits. We present tritify, an open-source runtime that executes the forward pass of real models -- decoder-only language models, Mixture-of-Experts decoders, and the Segment Anything 2.1 image/video stack -- with the entire run-time path in exact integer arithmetic; floating point is confined to offline quantization and the float reference used for verification. We make three separate claims and verify each. (1) Cross-hardware reproducibility: the integer path produces bit-identical output run to run, across CPU instruction-set architectures, and across CPU/GPU, carried by a reproducing SHA-256 of the output. (2) Decision fidelity: the integer path reproduces the float reference's decision on the models and inputs tested, with the numeric exceptions measured; per-layer fidelity through sixteen layers of OLMoE-1B-7B and of a 106-billion-parameter MoE shows no fidelity cliff. (3) Location independence: a model's computation can be split across instruction sets, CPU and GPU, and networked machines with zero effect on the output bits. GLM-4.5-Air (106,852,251,264 parameters, 427 GB of integer codes) generated its answer across three machines, none of which can hold its integer codes in RAM, bit-identically to a single-host reference. The consequence is verifiable distributed inference: an untrusted server or a fleet of devices runs the model while an open scalar oracle re-derives the exact bytes; a guarantee against a dishonest server is future work. We do not claim a per-device speed-up, bit-equality of floating-valued intermediates, or confidentiality. Code: https://github.com/pelloran-inc/tritify

fresh.title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
fresh.summary: Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are. We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness. The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.

fresh.title: Designing Collaborative Virtual Environments for Software Engineering Education
fresh.summary: Collaborative virtual environments offer opportunities to make software models available for shared inspection, but educational design and usability need to be examined separately from claims of learning effectiveness. This article presents MetaSEE, an approach connecting requirements guidance, a Web XR feature model, a reusable UML component, and a browser-based multiuser platform. We synthesize documented formative evaluations of the framework (16 participations), feature model (15), UML component (9), and platform (14). These counts represent evaluation participations; the same 12 developers took part in the first two evaluations. The principal platform study involved six teachers working individually and eight students working in four pairs through desktop or notebook computers, keyboard, and mouse. The documentary synthesis traces educational intentions to implemented features and reported difficulties. Participants identified potential value in shared modeling and simulation, alongside navigation, interaction, visualization, and distraction concerns. A numerical audit reconstructs a student System Usability Scale mean of 67.50 from published item frequencies, conflicting with the reported 79.38; an incomplete teacher item distribution prevents recovery of that group's overall mean. The contribution is a traceable account of educational design and formative limitations, with practical implications for onboarding, model readability, collaboration, and evaluation reporting. The evidence supports bounded feasibility and perceived usefulness, without establishing learning gains, sustained engagement, or adoption.

fresh.title: An Empirical Study on Improving LLM-Based Issue Classification through Domain-Informed Analysis
fresh.summary: Issue reports that describe Intrinsic Bugs, Extrinsic Bugs, and Not a Bug cases often use similar language, but they might point to different causes and require different maintenance actions. This makes three-way issue classification difficult for Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when prompt-based refinements begin to plateau. We study whether domain-informed analysis of LLM outputs can improve classification beyond prompt modification alone. Using 428 manually labeled issue reports, we evaluate six LLMs across 18 prompt configurations and analyze 7,704 model-generated rationales to identify recurring failure patterns in how models justify predictions, use evidence, and handle conflicting information. We translate these findings into a multi-stage pipeline that separates bug validity from bug origin. The pipeline improves macro F1 and Extrinsic Bug recall for five of the six models. The strongest pipeline configuration reaches 0.827 accuracy and 0.757 Extrinsic Bug recall, improving over the best-accuracy prompt-only baseline by +1.2 and +7.5 pp, respectively. The decomposition further reveals that bug origin classification is more reliable than validity, indicating that the bug-validity decision accounts for most of the remaining error. These results show that expert failure analysis can support more reliable LLM-based software engineering classifiers.

fresh.title: SPARK: Semantic-preserving Prompt Mutation for Code Generation using Consensus-based Verification Framework
fresh.summary: Automated code generation with large language models (LLMs) has improved in recent years. With the lack of test cases in real-world usages, generated code is not automatically verifiable and often requires manual validation. Previous studies have leveraged consensus verification, where code solutions and corresponding test cases are generated and evaluated based on functional consistency. Building on this, SPARK incorporates semantic-preserving mutations to problem descriptions such as paraphrasing, grammatical adjustments, function renaming, and other alterations to enhance the robustness and correctness of LLM-generated code. For each mutated description, SPARK generates a set of code solutions and test cases. These candidate solutions are evaluated using consensus-based verification, where the solutions' quality is measured by how consistently they pass generated tests. We assess the effectiveness of SPARK on three benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, BigCodeBench, and DLBench) across three LLMs (o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1-Basic, and Gemini-2.5-Pro). Our evaluation demonstrates that SPARK outperforms state-of-the-art consensus-based verification approaches by up to 4.1%. Our generalization experiment highlights the practical potential of SPARK as an effective strategy for enhancing the reliability and correctness of LLM-based code generation systems in scenarios where traditional validation resources are scarce, while our qualitative analysis shows insight into how SPARK's mutation helps LLMs generate better code solutions.

fresh.title: The AI Era's Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer's Token Spend Measures
fresh.summary: Organizations use engineers' token spend to monitor AI adoption, set budgets, and measure productivity, but the metric's relationship with engineering output is unclear. We link five weeks of token usage in coding agents to the commits of 404 engineers at JetBrains, and analyze a company survey of 412 employees. We find that token spend varied mostly between engineers, and which engineers spent the most stayed largely the same over the five weeks. Among weeks with similar commit counts, the 90th percentile of spend was 39 to 240 times the 10th. Within an engineer, doubling spend was associated with about 10% more commits. Available work metrics explained 38% of the variation in spend between engineers and 13% of the week-to-week variation within an engineer. In the survey, respondents in technical roles reported in nearly nine of ten agent evaluations using agents for tasks beyond coding, such as analysis, research, and planning. Token spend therefore measures how much engineers use agents across many kinds of work and not the outcome and value of that work. We recommend using token spend at most for resource accounting, and evaluating agent-assisted work with evidence about tasks and outcomes.

fresh.title: A Taxonomy of Failing Bug Reproduction Tests on SWT-Bench
fresh.summary: Automatic Program Repair (APR) tools require high-quality test generation models to validate candidate patches. Despite the advancements of automated bug reproduction testing tools, they continue to struggle with issues of higher complexity. These struggles may be caused by a framework's lack of problem-specific context. We address the unclassified nature of these framework failures by providing a taxonomy of bug reproduction tests. This study uses the AssertFlip and OpenHands frameworks, the two highest-scoring open-source tools on SWT-Bench Verified. The significance of model selection on the causes of failure is also explored by utilizing GPT-5-mini and GPT-4o-mini on both tools. The error traces of these frameworks are categorized to determine granular modes of failure. Through this process, mechanical and implementation failures were the most common failure classes. Overall, a tool's generation approach has a significant impact on precision and coverage, while the selection of the model alters the quality and quantity of generated tests. Specifically, more powerful models with higher reasoning capability tended to present fewer failures due to a lack of technical or problem-specific context. Our experiment also shows evidence that our taxonomy can be used as concrete guidance to augment the issue description to improve the generation quality.
